checks.name: policy_is_actually_updating
checks.detail: median approximate KL per update is 0.00545 against a 0.0001 floor. Below the floor the weights are barely moving and the run is a very expensive way to keep a random policy — which is what happened when the value gradient was 150x the policy's and one shared gradient clip scaled both by 0.0067.

checks.name: exploration_is_not_growing
checks.detail: policy entropy went -1.40 -> -1.76 (-0.37). A policy that is learning gets more decisive; rising entropy means the entropy bonus is beating the policy gradient, which on a Gaussian policy it will do indefinitely because entropy is unbounded above.

checks.name: exploration_matches_the_action_scale
checks.detail: holding the 40 m corner needs a normalised steering action of about 0.037; the policy searches with a standard deviation of 0.082, a ratio of 2.2x. Far above and the car saws the wheel off the road before it learns anything; far below and it never finds the behaviour at all.
checks.group: Is the search at the scale of the problem?

checks.name: the_two_action_dimensions_need_different_exploration
checks.detail: Steering rate and throttle have useful scales an order of magnitude apart — 0.037 of authority against the whole [-1, 1] interval — so a single exploration standard deviation cannot serve both. With one value small enough for the steering, the policy never sampled braking at all and sat at full throttle for half a million steps. This run uses [0.082, 0.223, 0.223, 0.223, 0.223].
checks.group: Is the search at the scale of the problem?

checks.name: exploration_covers_the_torque_vectoring_action
checks.detail: the torque-vectoring actions explore with standard deviations [0.211899995803833, 0.20730000734329224, 0.22120000422000885, 0.2093999981880188]. Below 0.001 and the policy has stopped trying anything but whatever it already does; above 2 the noise alone spans the entire action range and swamps the signal. A 1.1x spread across the 4 dimensions means at least one is being explored an order of magnitude less than the others — a policy that never learned to use one wheel would look exactly like this (F52's mismatched-exploration-scale failure, in a new action space).
checks.group: Is the search at the scale of the problem?

checks.name: the_task_is_completable
checks.detail: the car makes 19.3 m/s round this corner at the limit and starts the episode at 15.0 m/s. Starting above the corner speed means the first thing the policy must discover is hard braking, seconds before any consequence, against an immediate reward for going faster — configured that way it never completed a single lap in 250k steps.
checks.group: Is the task possible, and did it get solved?

checks.name: the_off_track_rate_came_down
checks.detail: episodes ending off the road went nan -> 0.00. A rate stuck at 1.00 means every episode is a crash and the policy has never seen the behaviour it is supposed to be reinforcing.
checks.group: Is the task possible, and did it get solved?

checks.name: the_critic_predicts_returns
checks.detail: explained variance over the last fifth of training has a median of +0.98. At zero the critic is no better than predicting the mean, which makes every advantage estimate noise and the policy gradient a random walk.

checks.name: the_deployed_policy_completes_the_task
checks.detail: the mean-action policy — the one you would ship — finishes 100% of laps and covers 394 m. Sampling its actions instead gives 100% and 393 m. **The deployed number is the result.** A run whose sampled policy performs well and whose mean action does not has not produced a driver; it has produced a policy whose competence lives in its own exploration noise, and the sampled figure describes something you cannot ship.
checks.group: Does the policy you would actually deploy work?

checks.name: greedy_and_stochastic_agree
checks.detail: mean-action rollouts reach 394 m and sampled rollouts reach 393 m, a 0% gap. A large gap means the behaviour depends on the exploration noise itself, so the deterministic policy you would ship is a different driver from the one the training curves describe.
checks.group: Does the policy you would actually deploy work?

checks.name: the_policy_stayed_inside_the_tire_model
checks.detail: the deployed policy's worst slip angle reached 7.8 deg against our 12 deg bound, with 0.0% of steps beyond it (sampled, for comparison: 9.3 deg, 0.0% of steps — training-time only). Every minimum-time solve in Seasons 1 and 2 constrains this; the environment deliberately does not, so the policy is free to operate where the Magic Formula is extrapolating and the forces are arithmetic rather than measurement.
checks.group: Did it stay inside the tire model?

checks.name: the_tire_file_s_own_load_range_was_respected
checks.detail: 0.0% of the deployed policy's steps left the tire file's own declared operating range (sampled: 0.0%). That bound is the file's, not ours, and outside it the model is not extrapolating from a fit — it has no fit.
checks.group: Did it stay inside the tire model?
